title: Check yourself: limitations and use cases for records

questions.stem: Every payment event carries an `eventId` and an `occurredAt`. A colleague writes `abstract class PaymentEvent` with those two fields and a constructor, then `record PaymentCaptured(String eventId, Instant occurredAt, long cents) extends PaymentEvent`. What happens, and where do the two shared values end up?

options.text: javac refuses the record, since a record names no superclass; the two values become components of each record, behind an interface
options.says: a record's superclass is always java.lang.Record and its header has no extends clause; shared shape goes into an interface whose methods the accessors implement

options.text: javac refuses the record, since the base class's fields are final; the two values become non-final fields that each record inherits
options.says: the refusal has nothing to do with the fields: a record can't extend any class

options.text: It compiles once PaymentEvent is an abstract record, since a record may extend another record that declares the two values as components
options.says: a record can't be abstract (modifier abstract not allowed here), and records are final, so no record extends another

options.text: It compiles once PaymentEvent is sealed and permits the records, since a sealed class lets records extend it and inherit both values
options.says: sealing a class doesn't lift the rule: a record still can't extend a class

origin.section: A Record Extends Only java.lang.Record, and Nothing Extends It

questions.stem: `record Route(List<Stop> stops)` has a slow `distanceKm()`. A developer adds `private double distance = -1;` to remember the result, javac rejects the line, and the developer marks the field `static`. It compiles. A 12 km route calls `distanceKm()` first, then a 40 km route does. What does the 40 km route report?

options.text: 12 km, since a static field holds one value for the whole class, and the first route filled it
options.says: a static field belongs to the class, so every route reads the value the first one stored

options.text: 12 km, since a record's accessors are generated once and cache what the first instance returned
options.says: the shared value comes from the static field, which belongs to the class, not from anything the record generates

options.text: 40 km, since a static field declared inside a record body gets one copy per instance
options.says: static means one per class, in a record as anywhere else

options.text: 40 km, since the record's equals takes the field into account and keeps the two values apart
options.says: equals compares components only, and a static field is not a component

origin.section: A Record's Only Instance State Is Its Header

questions.stem: An ORM loads each row by calling a no-arg constructor and then setting every field through reflection with `setAccessible(true)`. The team changes `Account` to `record Account(String iban, long balanceCents)` and adds `Account() { this(null, 0); }` so the ORM finds its constructor. What happens when the ORM loads a row?

options.text: The object is built, then setting a field fails, since a record's fields stay final to reflection with setAccessible(true)
options.says: Field.set on a record's field fails with 'Can not set final ... field' even after setAccessible(true)

options.text: The object is built, then the fields are filled, since setAccessible(true) lets reflection write to a final field too
options.says: setAccessible(true) allows writing a final instance field of an ordinary class, but not of a record

options.text: javac refuses the record, since a record may not declare a constructor of its own that takes no parameters
options.says: a non-canonical constructor is allowed when it starts with this(...), which this one does

options.text: javac refuses the record, since a record's no-arg constructor must assign the fields itself, not call this(...)
options.says: it is the other way round: javac refuses a non-canonical constructor that doesn't start with this(...)

origin.section: A Framework That Builds an Object Empty, Then Fills It, Can't Build a Record

questions.stem: A hotel keeps the guests who are in the building in a `HashSet<Guest>`, with `record Guest(String name, String birthDate)`. Two unrelated guests, both named Jane Doe and born on "1988-07-14", check in to rooms 112 and 418, and each check-in adds a `new Guest(...)` to the set. How many entries does the set hold?

options.text: One, since the record's equals and hashCode come from its components, the same for both guests
options.says: a record's equals compares components, so two people with the same data are one entry

options.text: One, since the JVM shares equal record instances, so both check-ins add one and the same object
options.says: the two objects are distinct, as the page notes; they are one entry because they are equal, not because they are the same object

options.text: Two, since each check-in creates its own object, and a HashSet keeps objects created separately
options.says: a HashSet keeps one of any two equal elements, however they were created

options.text: Two, since a record's hashCode mixes the object's identity into the hash of its components
options.says: a record's hashCode is derived from its components only; there is no identity in it

origin.section: Keep a Class for Identity, Changing State, or Many Optional Parts
